Slides accessible here: ` https://pengyunc.quarto.pub/week7/` ## Economics Honours Info Session - Date: Tuesday 23 September, 12pm--1pm - Venue: The Spot (Room 4014) - Program Enquiries: - Aaron Barkley (Honours Coordinator) - Email: `aaron.barkley@unimelb.edu.au` - **Application Deadline for 2026 intake: **15 November 2025 ## Recap of Tutorial 6 In Tutorial 6, the ADF test indicated that the $\log(CPI_{t})$ series contains a unit root. :::{.incremental} - This means we cannot just remove the trend and fit an ARMA model. - $\to$ We need to first difference the $\log(CPI_{t})$ series to render it stationary. - We then ran the ADF test with drift on $\Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ and the null hypothesis of a unit root was rejected at 5\% level. - $\to$ $\Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ can be modeled as an ARMA process. - So we proceeded with selecting the optimal ARMA($p,q$) order for $\Delta\log(CPI_{t})$ using a grid search of $p=0,\dots,4$ and $q=0,\dots,4$. - **So what is the purpose of ADF test here?** - To assist with selecting $d=0$ or $d=1$ in an ARIMA model. - We may wonder: Can we let an information criterion (AIC or AICc) select $d$ automatically, alongside $p$ and $q$? - **This tutorial:** Maybe we can replace that decision with AIC, just like we pick $p$ and $q$? $\to$ we will examine this idea with a simulation ::: ## This tutorial {auto-animate="true"} In this tutorial we will use simulation to explore the possible usefulness of the AIC for deciding whether to difference a time series or not, in comparison to the conventional ADF tests.
:::{.callout-note title = "Simulation Setting"} :::{.incremental} - Use a sample size of $n=100$. - Fit an AR model with fixed order $p=2$ and with intercept only: $$\mathrm{ARIMA}(2,0,0):\qquad Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\phi_{1}Y_{t-1}+\phi_{2}Y_{t-2}+U_{t}$$ - A restricted version of this model is to take a first difference of $Y_{t}$: $$\mathrm{ARIMA}(1,1,0):\qquad\Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\psi_{1}\Delta Y_{t-1}+U_{t}$$ - Selection Criteria: Select ARIMA(1,1,0) if $\operatorname{AIC}_{\operatorname{ARIMA(1,1,0)}}<\operatorname{AIC}_{\operatorname{ARIMA(2,0,0)}}$. - We will compare the ADF and AIC approaches in two ways: i. proportion of “correct” choice of differencing ii. resulting one-step-ahead forecasting performance. ::: ::: ## Simulation: Data Generating Process {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-note title="Data Generating Process"} The data generating process for the simulation will be $$Y_{t}=\phi Y_{t-1}+U_{t},\qquad U_{t}\sim\text{i.i.d. N}(0,1)$$ with $n=100$ and $\phi_{1}=1,0.95,0.9,0.85,0.8,0.7,0.6,0.5$. :::
- For setting up the code, we select $\phi=0.9$ (without loss of generality), but we can change it later. - The true underlying process is actually AR(1), although we will fit AR(2). - When $\phi_{1}\ne 1$, no differencing is needed for $Y_{t}$ $\to$ the correct choice is AR(2) - When $\phi_{1}=1$, $Y_{t}$ is a unit-root process $\to$ the correct choice is ARIMA(1,1,0) ## Initialisation {auto-animate="true"} Load libraries: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(forecast) library(urca) ``` :::

Estimate ARIMA(2,0,0) and ARIMA(1,1,0) models for Y # Estimation of AR(2) model ARIMA200 <- lm(Y[t]~Y[t-1]+Y[t-2]) # Estimation of ARIMA(1,1,0) model DY <- Y[t]-Y[t-1] DY1 <- Y[t-1]-Y[t-2] ARIMA110 <- lm(DY[t]~DY[t-1]) ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip title="Notes"} - Recall we set `t = (p+1):n`, and `p = 2` is the AR order. - **Why do we use `lm` instead of `Arima` this time?** - This is because when $\phi_{1}=1$, the series is not stationary. - `Arima` command enforces a stationarity check and will return an error in this case. - Beneath the surface `Arima` is attempting to do “maximum likelihood” estimation, which can be tricky in non-stationary settings, while `lm` is doing least squares which continues to be workable. ::: ## Simulation Code {auto-animate="true"} **Part c:** Compute one step ahead forecast errors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # c. Compute and store 1-step-ahead forecast errors for each model # in columns 1 and 2 of ForecastErrors b1 <- ARIMA110$coefficients ForecastErrors[r,1] <- Yf - (Y[n]+b1[1]+b1[2]*DY[length(DY)]) b2 <- ARIMA200$coefficients ForecastErrors[r,2] <- Yf - (b2[1]+b2[2]*Y[n]+b2[3]*Y[n-1]) ``` ::: :::{.callout-tip title="Notes"} - `Yf` is the actual 1-step-ahead observation ($Y_{n+1}$) - Forecast errors are computed as: $$\hat{U}_{n+1}=Y_{n+1}-\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n}]$$ where the forecasting equations are: $$\begin{aligned}\text{ARIMA(1,1,0):}&& \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n}]&=Y_{n}+\color{blue}{\widehat{\Delta Y}_{n+1}}\,\color{black}{=Y_{n}\,+}\,\color{blue}{(\hat{\beta}_{0}+\hat{\psi}_{1}\Delta Y_{n})}\\ \text{ARIMA(2,0,0):}&& \hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{n+1}\mid\mathscr{Y}_{n}]&=\hat{\beta}_{0}+\hat{\phi}_{1}Y_{n}+\hat{\phi}_{2}Y_{n-1} \end{aligned}$$ ::: ## Simulation Code {auto-animate="true"} **Part d:** Perform the ADF test to check for differencing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # d. ADF test on Y, store decision in column 1 of ur # ADF test with drift, lags=1 (include one augmenting term) adf_tstat = ur.df(Y, type="drift", lags=1)@teststat[1] ur[r,1] <- 1*(punitroot(adf_tstat, N=n, trend="c", statistic="t")>0.05) # Store forecast error of ADF-chosen model in col 3 of ForecastErrors # If ADF test selects unit root use ARIMA110 forecast error: if (ur[r,1]==1){ ForecastErrors[r,3] <- ForecastErrors[r,1] } else { # otherwise use ARIMA200 forecast error: ForecastErrors[r,3] <- ForecastErrors[r,2] } ``` :::
Recall the hypotheses of the ADF test are: \begin{align} H_{0}:&\;\varphi=0& &\text{($Y_{t}$ has a unit root)}\\ H_{1}:&\;\varphi<0& &\text{($Y_{t}$ does not have a unit root)} \end{align} thus if $p>0.05 \implies H_{0}$ is maintained, ADF suggests ARIMA(1,1,0) $\to$ **record 1** ## Simulation Code {auto-animate="true"} **Part e:** Use AIC to check for differencing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # e. AIC choice between ARIMA(2,0,0) and ARIMA(1,1,0) # Store decision in column 2 of ur ur[r,2] <- 1*(AIC(ARIMA110) Recall that when AIC is used, we select ARIMA(1,1,0) if $$\operatorname{AIC}_{\operatorname{ARIMA(1,1,0)}}<\operatorname{AIC}_{\operatorname{ARIMA(2,0,0)}}$$ if this is satisfied, store `ur[r,2]=1`, and store the forecast error of ARIMA(1,1,0) under `ForecastErrors[r,4]`. ## Simulation Results To make the results reproducible, we set a random seed at `42`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(42) ``` :::

Set up two extra storage matrices for model selection results and RMSEs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Stores model selection results for each phi1 (should be 8x2) my_ur = matrix(nrow=length(phi1_values), ncol=2) colnames(my_ur) <- c("ADF", "AIC") rownames(my_ur) <- paste0("phi1=", phi1_values) # Stores RMSE results for each phi1 (should be 8x4) my_RMSE = matrix(nrow=length(phi1_values), ncol=4) colnames(my_RMSE) <- c("ARIMA110", "ARIMA200", "ADF", "AIC") rownames(my_RMSE) <- paste0("phi1=", phi1_values) ``` ::: ## Simulation: Looping over all $\phi_{1}$ values {auto-animate="true"} Next, add an extra layer of `for` loop for `phi1` ($\phi_{1}$) values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (i in 1:length(phi1_values)){ phi1 = phi1_values[i] ur <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=2) colnames(ur) <- c("ADF", "AIC") ForecastErrors <- matrix(nrow=reps, ncol=4) colnames(ForecastErrors) <- c("ARIMA110", "ARIMA200", "ADF", "AIC") set.seed(42) for (r in 1:reps){ # steps a-e code goes here... } my_ur[i,] <- apply(ur, 2, mean)*100 my_RMSE[i,] <- sqrt(apply(ForecastErrors^2, 2, mean)) } ``` ::: ## Results {auto-animate="true"} ::: {.cell} ::: Running the completed code produces the following results: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(my_ur) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ADF AIC phi1=1 95.8 93.3 phi1=0.95 89.4 84.6 phi1=0.9 70.6 63.5 phi1=0.85 44.3 37.8 phi1=0.8 20.7 19.4 phi1=0.7 2.3 3.7 phi1=0.6 0.2 0.9 phi1=0.5 0.0 0.1 ``` ::: :::

:::{.incremental} - In this experiment the AIC demonstrates some tendency to find a unit root in a time series a little less than the ADF test, regardless of whether or not there is a unit root. - When $\phi_{1}=1$ (unit root) the ADF test finds a unit root 95.8% of the time, consistent (approximately) with the 5% significance level of the test. The AIC finds a unit root 93.3% of the time. This does not appear to be a huge difference on the surface. - When $\phi_{1}<1$ the difference between the ADF and AIC selection proportions becomes as high as about 7%. A noticeable but not huge difference. The implications of this difference are explored using forecast performance. - Conclusion: Overall the AIC provides a reasonable way to distinguish between unit root or not in this experiment. ::: ## Results: RMSE {auto-animate="true"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} print(round(my_RMSE,4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ARIMA110 ARIMA200 ADF AIC phi1=1 0.9877 1.0039 0.9912 0.9904 phi1=0.95 1.0300 1.0141 1.0328 1.0304 phi1=0.9 1.0512 1.0258 1.0471 1.0460 phi1=0.85 1.0887 1.0474 1.0744 1.0721 phi1=0.8 1.0889 1.0275 1.0389 1.0458 phi1=0.7 1.1163 1.0521 1.0599 1.0575 phi1=0.6 1.0941 1.0042 1.0076 1.0108 phi1=0.5 1.1554 1.0161 1.0161 1.0164 ``` ::: :::
:::{.incremental} - Many of the RMSEs are approximately the same. The biggest differences occur when is away from 1, i.e. $\phi_{1}=0.5,0.6$. - In this case the ARIMA(1,1,0) model is clearly misspecified, and its forecasting performance suffers. - However both ADF and AIC do a good job in selecting the correct model here. - When $\phi_{1}=1$ the RMSEs are all roughly the same. This is interesting - if there is a unit root then it doesn’t matter what we do, at least for one-step-ahead forecasting. - Overall the RMSEs for the ADF and AIC methods are practically the same. There is no benefit in making this decision in this experiment in using the specialised ADF, we could just as easily have used the AIC. - Maybe interestingly, there is a “grey area’ around $\phi_{1}=0.95$ to $\phi_{1}=0.85$, where the selected models do worse than the ARIMA(2,0,0), although the RMSE differences are small. ::: ## Final Note :::{.incremental} - The most important thing is to understand the simulation approach. - We are using simulation to replicate the frequentist statistical concept of a sampling distribution and hence to obtain experimental evidence on the performance of some tests and forecasts. - Limitation: We have only tried a limited range of data generating processes and models and so the current results are only specific to that setting. ::: ## {data-background-color="#000F46"}
